rationale: The book's core identification — that 'righteousness' in Scripture denotes the doing of God's commandments (righteous acts performed), not a vague moral quality nor solely a forensic verdict received — is directly stated by the three texts printed with the entry: Deuteronomy 6:25 explicitly defines righteousness as observing to do all the commandments; Psalm 119:172 equates the commandments themselves with righteousness; and 1 John 3:7 warns against precisely the deception the book targets ('he that doeth righteousness is righteous'). Within the evidence bundle, Revelation 19:8's Greek plural dikaiōmata ('righteous acts of the saints,' as ASV/ESV/NASB/NIV render it) is a decisive textual detail: the wedding garment the whole chapter turns on is explicitly composed of deeds, which the imputed-status counter must flatten into a singular credited status against the grammar of the verse. The book also pre-empts the strongest counter-texts within its bundle: Isaiah 64:6 (filthy rags) is read in context as deeds stained by the doer's sin rather than obedience being filth, and the 'given' clauses (Isa 61:10; Rev 19:8; Eph 2:10; Luke 15:22) are absorbed by the book's granted-then-worn structure, so grace is not denied but relocated. The forensic counter explains the exhortations to keep, wash, and not defile garments (Rev 3:4; 16:15; Jude 23; Zech 3:4) only awkwardly — commands to maintain a garment make little sense if the garment is a once-declared status independent of conduct. The book's negative clause denies only exclusivity ('a verdict only received'), so texts about righteousness being credited do not falsify it. Secondary elaborations (helmet-as-Yeshuah wordplay, kanaph/fringe linkage, the muzzling philology, Daniel 12:4 application) are suggestive but not proven to the same standard, hence CORE_ONLY.
book_core_identification: Righteousness is the doing of God's commandments — enacted obedience (righteous acts), granted by God and performed by the person, symbolized as a garment woven of deeds; it is not merely an imputed legal status passively received.
book_secondary_elaborations: The wedding garment of Matthew 22 is identified as the fine linen of Revelation 19:8, i.e., righteous acts
The garment is covenant-wear: Ezekiel 16's spread skirt equates covering nakedness with entering covenant
Foot-washing (John 13) as the daily cleansing of conduct distinct from the one-time bath of baptism
Fig leaves and the fruitless fig tree as self-made counterfeit righteousness
The armor of God (Eph 6) as God's own war-dress from Isaiah 59:17, each piece a defined symbol
The helmet of salvation as the helmet of Yeshuah covering the head/mind, via Psalm 140:7 and 1 Cor 11:3
Nakedness as covenant exposure rather than nudity (Rev 3:17; 16:15; Isa 47:3; 2 Cor 5:3)
The muzzled (phimoō) speechlessness of the garmentless man as judicial silencing
strongest_counter_interpretation: The classic Protestant forensic reading: righteousness in its dominant theological sense is a legal standing before God imputed to the believer through faith in Christ, apart from works (Gen 15:6; Rom 4:3-8; Rom 5:17-19; Phil 3:9; 2 Cor 5:21). On this reading the garment imagery (Isa 61:10; Zech 3:3-5) pictures a righteousness bestowed as covering, not woven from the wearer's deeds; Deut 6:25 and 1 John 3:7 describe a subordinate ethical sense or the fruit/evidence of the imputed status rather than the term's core meaning; and Isaiah 64:6 shows human deeds cannot constitute righteousness at all.
counter_core_identification: Righteousness is fundamentally a right standing before God — a status declared and credited by God on the basis of faith in Christ, not constituted by the doing of commandments.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that righteousness is constituted by performed obedience: if righteousness is essentially a credited forensic status received apart from works (Rom 4:5-6; Phil 3:9), then it cannot be identified with 'the doing of God's commandments,' and the garment must symbolize a bestowed status rather than the law kept and worn. Both identifications cannot be true of the same referent as the term's core meaning.
counter_case: Genesis 15:6 and Romans 4:3-8 present righteousness as counted/credited on the basis of faith, explicitly 'without works'
Philippians 3:9 contrasts 'mine own righteousness, which is of the law' unfavorably with 'the righteousness which is of God by faith'
Isaiah 64:6 declares 'all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags,' suggesting human deeds cannot constitute saving righteousness
The garment is repeatedly 'given' (Isa 61:10; Zech 3:4; Luke 15:22; Rev 19:8 'it was given unto her'), fitting bestowal of status rather than accumulation of deeds
2 Corinthians 5:21 speaks of becoming the righteousness of God 'in him,' locating righteousness in union with Christ, not in commandment-keeping
book_explanatory_advantages: Deuteronomy 6:25 is an explicit lexical definition — 'it shall be our righteousness, if we observe to do all these commandments' — that the counter must demote to a secondary sense
Psalm 119:172 flatly equates the commandments with righteousness
1 John 3:7 is framed as a warning against being deceived on exactly this point: doing righteousness is what makes one righteous

Revelation 19:8's plural dikaiōmata ('righteous acts of the saints') defines the very garment at the marriage of the Lamb as deeds, not a status; the book documents the KJV's narrowing and the major modern versions' agreement
The exhortations to keep, wash, and not defile garments (Rev 3:4; 16:15; Jude 23; Zech 3:4) presuppose ongoing conduct affecting the garment, which the book's reading explains natively

The book absorbs the counter's best texts: Isa 64:6 is read in its own context (the doer unclean, not the deed evil), and the 'given' clauses are integrated via Eph 2:10 (deeds ordained by God, granted then worn)
Job 29:14 ('I put on righteousness, and it clothed me') and Rev 22:14 ('they that do his commandments') independently attest righteousness as worn conduct
The two-stage structure from Ezekiel 16 (covenant covering first, then clothing) explains why the prodigal receives the robe before any deeds, defusing an apparent counter-example
counter_explanatory_advantages: Better accounts for the Pauline credited-apart-from-works texts (Gen 15:6; Rom 4:3-8; Phil 3:9), none of which the supplied bundle directly engages
Explains why the garment language emphasizes divine bestowal ('he hath clothed me,' 'it was given unto her') with a simpler single mechanism
Fits the broad Protestant consensus reading of Romans 1-5 without requiring a distinction between senses of righteousness across corpora
decisive_sources: Deuteronomy 6:25 — explicit definitional equation of righteousness with doing the commandments
1 John 3:7 — 'he that doeth righteousness is righteous,' framed as a warning against deception
Revelation 19:8 — dikaiōmata, plural 'righteous acts of the saints,' identifying the wedding garment's fabric as deeds
Revelation 3:4 and 16:15 — garments that must be kept undefiled, presupposing conduct
Isaiah 64:6 read in context — the stain is the doer's sin, not the obedience itself
Job 29:14 — righteousness put on as clothing by the one who does it
unresolved_objections: The supplied material never directly addresses Genesis 15:6, Romans 4:3-8, or Philippians 3:9, where righteousness is counted by faith apart from works; the book's 'granted then worn' framework can accommodate these, but the reconciliation is not demonstrated in the bundle

The entry's definition may over-generalize a genuine deed-sense (dominant in Deut, Psalms, 1 John, Revelation's garment texts) across all uses of the term, including Pauline forensic contexts where the word plausibly carries a status sense

Several symbolic elaborations (helmet as the name Yeshuah, the kanaph/fringe covenant linkage, phimoō as judicial muzzling, the Daniel 12:4 application) rest on wordplay and thematic association rather than the multi-witness standard the book itself sets
